description: Free trade, tariffs, quotas, free-trade agreements, the EU single market, and the effects of globalisation.
content_html:
What is Free Trade?

Free trade means countries can buy and sell goods and services across borders without government-imposed barriers. When a UK consumer buys a Spanish orange or a French car, that transaction happens because the sellers can access the UK market freely — and UK exporters, such as pharmaceutical or financial services firms, can reach customers abroad on the same terms. Free trade is the opposite of protectionism, where governments deliberately limit foreign competition to shield domestic industries.

Key Fact

The two main trade barriers are tariffs (taxes on imported goods that raise their price and make domestic goods more competitive) and quotas (legal limits on the quantity of a good that can be imported). Both reduce the volume of trade and can trigger retaliatory barriers from trading partners.

Arguments For and Against Free Trade

The case for free trade rests on the idea of comparative advantage. Countries that focus on producing what they are relatively best at — and then trade — can all end up with more goods at lower prices than if each tried to produce everything itself. For UK consumers, free trade means access to a wider range of goods (imported electronics, clothing, food) at prices that competition drives down.

Free trade also benefits UK exporters. When foreign markets are open, UK firms — from car manufacturers to software companies — can sell to billions of customers rather than just the domestic market of around 68–69 million people at home. Larger export markets allow firms to grow, gain economies of scale, and invest in new products.

However, free trade is not without costs. Domestic industries that cannot compete with cheaper foreign goods may shrink, leading to unemployment in those sectors. When a steel plant closes because cheaper imports undercut it, the workers who lose their jobs may find it hard to retrain quickly — a real human cost, even if consumers benefit from lower prices. Some argue that certain industries (food production, for example) should be protected for reasons of national security, so the country is not entirely dependent on foreign supply.

A tariff is a tax that the government charges on an imported good. If the government puts a 20% tariff on imported steel, foreign steel becomes more expensive in the UK and domestic producers can compete more easily. The government also raises revenue from the tariff. A quota limits the number of units that can be imported in a given period — for example, no more than five million tonnes of steel per year. Once the quota is reached, no more can be imported at any price. Quotas do not raise government revenue but they cap the volume of competition directly. Both measures raise prices for consumers and can provoke other countries to retaliate with their own barriers.

Free-Trade Agreements and the Role of the EU

Countries can formalise their commitment to open trade through a free-trade agreement (FTA). An FTA removes or lowers tariffs and quotas between the signing countries, making it easier for businesses on both sides to sell to each other. The more countries involved, the larger the market and the greater the potential gains.

The European Union (EU) is one of the most significant examples of deep economic integration. Its single market goes beyond a standard FTA: it removes not only tariffs but also most non-tariff barriers (such as different product regulations) so that goods, services, capital and workers can move freely among member states. Firms in EU countries effectively operate within one large home market of hundreds of millions of consumers. The EU also operates a customs union, meaning all members apply the same tariffs to goods coming in from outside the EU, and trade between members is tariff-free.

Key Fact

In a free-trade agreement, member countries remove barriers to trade with each other but each country sets its own tariffs on goods from outside. In a customs union, members also apply a common external tariff to non-members. The EU is a customs union as well as a single market.

For a country inside the EU, the single market provides tariff-free access to a huge pool of customers and suppliers. Businesses benefit from common product standards (a UK firm does not need to redesign its product for each EU country). Workers can move freely, helping employers fill skill shortages. Foreign direct investment flows more easily across borders. On the other hand, membership requires accepting common rules and regulations, contributing to the EU budget, and allowing free movement of people — each of which has political and economic trade-offs. When the UK left the EU, British exporters faced new customs checks and paperwork that had not previously existed, increasing costs for businesses trading with the EU.

Globalisation — What It Is and Why It Has Grown

Globalisation refers to the way national economies have become more integrated over recent decades. The growth of globalisation has been driven by several forces. Improvements in technology — container shipping, the internet, jet travel — have reduced the cost and time of moving goods, services and information around the world. The spread of free-trade agreements has lowered the legal barriers to trade. And the rise of multinational corporations (MNCs) has created global supply chains that link factories, workers and consumers across continents.

Consider a smartphone assembled in Asia, using components from a dozen different countries, designed by engineers in California, marketed globally and sold in a UK high street. That product represents globalisation in action: specialisation on a world scale, coordinated by multinationals chasing lower costs and larger markets.

Benefits of Globalisation

For UK consumers, globalisation means cheaper goods and more choice. Clothing, electronics and food are more affordable because they are produced where costs are lowest. For UK producers, global markets mean potential customers everywhere — a small British software firm or whisky distillery can reach buyers worldwide. For workers in developing countries, MNC investment can bring jobs, wages and technology transfer that raise living standards, even if wages are lower than in developed countries.

Drawbacks of Globalisation

Globalisation also creates losers. UK workers in manufacturing sectors that face low-cost foreign competition may find their wages squeezed or their jobs disappearing entirely — a process sometimes called deindustrialisation. When firms move production to lower-cost countries (offshoring), UK communities that depended on those factories can be left with structural unemployment that is hard to reverse.

There are also broader concerns. Global supply chains can be fragile — a disruption in one country ripples through the whole chain. Moral and ethical questions arise when MNCs operate in countries with weaker labour or environmental protections: lower wages, longer hours or less stringent pollution rules effectively export those lower standards. Consumers may unwittingly buy goods produced under conditions they would not accept at home. Some argue that the gains from globalisation have been unevenly distributed, benefiting shareholders and consumers of cheap goods more than the workers displaced by it.

MNCs play a central role in globalisation. They invest across borders (foreign direct investment), bringing capital, technology and jobs to host countries. For a developing country, an MNC setting up a factory can boost exports, raise wages and transfer skills. However, MNCs also attract criticism. They may shift profits to low-tax countries (tax avoidance), reducing tax revenue for host governments. They can undercut local businesses that cannot match their scale or prices. And if trading conditions change, an MNC can relocate production relatively easily, leaving workers and communities behind. The power of large MNCs can sometimes exceed that of the governments of the countries they operate in.
exam_tip_html: When the command word is Evaluate on a globalisation or free-trade question, don’t just list pros and cons — you must compare them and reach a supported judgement. A strong judgement uses “it depends on” logic: for example, the impact of globalisation depends on who you are (consumer vs. displaced worker), which country is involved (developed vs. developing), and the time period (short-run disruption vs. long-run gains). For a 6-mark Analyse question, build a chain of reasoning: “free trade lowers import prices → consumers have more purchasing power → domestic spending rises → GDP may increase.” Avoid vague phrases like “the economy gets better” — name the variable that changes and say which direction it moves and why.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Free trade removes barriers such as tariffs (taxes on imports) and quotas (limits on import volumes), enabling countries to specialise and consumers to access cheaper, more varied goods — but it can cause job losses in industries that cannot compete.
  • Free-trade agreements, including the EU single market and customs union, reduce barriers between member countries and give businesses access to larger markets with common rules.
  • Globalisation — driven by technology, MNCs and falling trade barriers — has raised living standards and created jobs in many countries, but has also led to deindustrialisation in some sectors and raises moral questions about labour and environmental standards in global supply chains.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a tariff?
A) A legal limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported
B) A tax placed on imported goods to raise their price
C) A treaty that removes all trade barriers between two countries
D) A subsidy paid to domestic firms to help them export
practice_questions.marks: B) A tax placed on imported goods to raise their price [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A country imports 200,000 units of a good at £5 each. The government then imposes a 20% tariff. Calculate the new price consumers pay per unit and the total additional cost to consumers if they still buy 200,000 units.
practice_questions.marks: New price per unit: £5 × 1.20 = £6 [1 mark for correct method/formula]; total additional cost: 200,000 × £1 = £200,000 [1 mark for correct answer of £200,000].

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit of free-trade agreements for businesses.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a benefit (e.g. access to larger export markets without tariff barriers); 1 mark for developing the point (e.g. this allows firms to sell to more customers and increase revenue); 1 mark for a further development or real-world example (e.g. a UK car manufacturer can export to partner countries without paying tariffs, reducing costs and making the product more price-competitive abroad).

practice_questions.text: A UK clothing manufacturer is considering whether to move production to a lower-cost country overseas. Explain how this decision could benefit and harm workers in the UK.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a harm to UK workers (e.g. job losses in the UK factory); 1 mark for developing the harm (e.g. structural unemployment may result as the skills of displaced workers may not match demand in other industries); 1 mark for identifying a benefit (e.g. UK consumers benefit from lower clothing prices as production costs fall); 1 mark for developing the benefit (e.g. lower prices increase real purchasing power for UK households, raising living standards).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a rise in globalisation might affect UK consumers and UK workers in manufacturing industries.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Sustained chain of reasoning covering both consumers and workers, with a clear explanation of how cause and effect operate in each case. For example: globalisation lowers the cost of imported goods → prices fall for consumers → purchasing power and real incomes rise → consumers can buy more goods and services. For manufacturing workers: greater competition from low-cost producers overseas → demand for labour in UK manufacturing falls → wages may fall or jobs disappear → structural unemployment rises → communities reliant on those industries suffer long-term. Response makes clear that the same process benefits one group while harming another.

Secure (3–4 marks): Clear points about both consumers and workers with some development, but the chain of reasoning may not be fully sustained or may lack a connecting mechanism.

Developing (2 marks): One side covered with some development, or both sides mentioned at a surface level only.

Emerging (1 mark): Simple assertion that globalisation is good or bad, with no developed explanation.

practice_questions.text:
'The benefits of globalisation outweigh the drawbacks for the UK economy.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support (benefits outweigh drawbacks):
• Consumers gain access to cheaper and more varied goods as firms produce where costs are lowest — lower prices raise real incomes and living standards.
• UK exporters benefit from access to global markets, enabling economies of scale and higher profits that support investment and jobs in export sectors.
• Foreign direct investment from MNCs brings capital, technology and employment — UK regions that attract inward investment benefit from new jobs and skills.
• Competition from imports forces domestic firms to innovate and improve efficiency, making the economy more productive in the long run.

Arguments against (drawbacks may be significant):
• Deindustrialisation — UK manufacturing has declined as production shifted overseas, causing structural unemployment in some regions that has proved persistent and hard to reverse through retraining alone.
• Benefits are unevenly distributed: shareholders and consumers of cheap goods gain most, while workers in sectors exposed to low-cost competition lose jobs or face wage stagnation.
• Moral and ethical concerns — global supply chains may involve low wages, poor working conditions or weaker environmental standards in producing countries; UK consumers may be indirectly supporting these practices.
• Global supply chains can be fragile — a shock in one country (such as a pandemic or natural disaster) can disrupt UK supply of key goods, threatening national security and resilience.

Judgement: Mastering (10–12 marks): Both sides developed with supporting chains of reasoning. A supported judgement that addresses 'it depends on' factors: which sector/region is considered, the time horizon (short-run disruption vs long-run gain), and whether policy can redistribute the gains (e.g. through retraining schemes or progressive taxation). The strongest answers recognise that net benefit is plausible in aggregate but the distribution of that benefit is deeply uneven.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides covered with development; judgement reached but may be asserted rather than fully argued.

Developing (4–6 marks): Both sides mentioned but one side is notably weaker; or development is present on one side only.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Simple list of pros and cons with minimal development; no or superficial judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What is a quota in the context of international trade?
options: A tax on imported goods that raises their price
A limit on the total value of exports allowed per year
A legal limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported
A subsidy paid to domestic exporters

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes the EU single market?
options: A tariff applied to goods from outside the EU only
An agreement allowing free movement of goods, services, capital and people between member states
A common currency shared by all EU member states
A quota system limiting imports from non-EU countries

knowledge_checks.q: The process by which the world's economies become more connected through trade, technology and the movement of capital is called _____.
A company that produces and sells goods or services across several different countries is called a _____ corporation.
Match each trade term to its correct meaning:
right: A tax on imported goods designed to raise their price
A treaty between countries that removes or reduces trade barriers
Government policies that restrict imports to protect domestic industries

flashcard_questions.a: Trade between countries with no tariffs, quotas or other government-imposed barriers.
A tax on imported goods that raises their price, making domestic goods more competitive.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a quota in international trade?
flashcard_questions.a: A legal limit on the quantity of a good that can be imported in a given period.
Government policies that restrict imports to shield domestic industries from foreign competition.
A treaty between countries that removes or reduces tariffs and quotas between them.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the EU single market allow that a standard FTA does not?
flashcard_questions.a: Free movement of goods, services, capital and workers — removing non-tariff barriers too.

flashcard_questions.q: In a customs union, what do all member countries share that they do not in a basic FTA?
flashcard_questions.a: A common external tariff on goods imported from outside the union.
The increasing economic integration of the world through trade, technology, MNCs and capital flows.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two forces that have driven the growth of globalisation.
flashcard_questions.a: Improvements in technology (internet, container shipping) and the spread of free-trade agreements.
A company that produces and sells goods or services across several countries.

flashcard_questions.q: How can globalisation harm UK manufacturing workers?
flashcard_questions.a: Lower-cost foreign competition can reduce demand for their labour, causing job losses and structural unemployment.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one benefit of globalisation for UK consumers.
flashcard_questions.a: Access to cheaper and more varied imported goods, raising purchasing power.
The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than a trading partner.
A long-run decline in a country's manufacturing sector, often linked to competition from lower-cost overseas producers.

glossary_terms.definition: Trade between countries that is not restricted by tariffs, quotas or other government-imposed barriers.
Government measures that restrict the flow of imports into a country, such as tariffs, quotas and regulations.
The ability of a country, firm or worker to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than a rival.
Reductions in average costs that come from producing on a larger scale.
A treaty between two or more countries that removes or reduces trade barriers between them.
The increasing interconnection of the world's economies through the growth of trade, communication, technology and the movement of capital and people.
A company that operates in several countries, producing and selling goods or services across international borders.
